title: The Poem That Killed a King? | Nandi Kalambakam Curse #shorts

lines.text: Can a poem kill a king?
A Tamil legend says one did. The king was the Pallava ruler Nandivarman the Third, in the eight hundreds.
lines.caps: a Tamil *legend | says one *did | the *Pallava | *Nandivarman | the *Third | 800s *CE.

lines.text: His half brothers, the story goes, fought him for the throne, and lost.
lines.caps: his half *brothers | the *story goes | *fought him | and *lost.

lines.text: So one of them turned to words.
He wrote a poem praising the king, the Nandi Kalambakam, but hid a curse inside its verses, called aram.
lines.caps: a *poem | praising the *king | *Nandi | *Kalambakam | a *curse | inside | called *aram.

lines.text: The king loved poetry. The legend says he sat to hear it under a row of pavilions.
lines.caps: he *loved | poetry | the *legend says | a row of | *pavilions.

lines.text: With every verse, a pavilion caught fire. He moved to the next, and the next.
lines.caps: every *verse | a pavilion | caught *fire | the *next | and the *next.

lines.text: When the last verse ended, the story says, the king burned with it.
lines.caps: the *last verse | the story *says | the king | *burned.

lines.text: Now the record. The poem is real, and praises a real Nandivarman, victor at Tellaru. But no inscription tells of a cursed death, and scholars doubt a brother wrote it.
lines.caps: now the *record | the poem | is *real | victor at *Tellaru | no *inscription | a *cursed death? | scholars *doubt | a brother *wrote it.

lines.text: Murder by poetry, or a story to explain how a king died? Tell me below. Then look again: the poem survived. The king did not.
